sections.title: From emotion to sensation to impulse
When the problem keeps coming back

blocks.p: When it comes to trauma relief, what is unstucking? What are pendulation and titration? And what do impulses have to do with any of this?
One of my course students sent me this question:

q: Unstucking means eventually one won't experience that stuck energy, for example, freeze, anymore, or that with this pendulation and titration practice, one is going to build a stronger vagal brake and acquire more self-regulation tools? I'm confused because I keep thinking that acting on my impulse of shouting, for example, whenever I get caught up in a freeze state, will help release this frozen energy, but I keep falling back into this state.

blocks.p: There are three questions in there, and I'm going to take them one at a time.
"Unstucking" is kind of a Justin-specific term, so I'd better be clear about what I mean by it.

Does it mean not experiencing the stuck energy anymore, the energy that comes along with a stuck state like freeze? If you're having some extreme success and truly getting 100% unstuck, then sure, I guess you may not experience that stuck, frozen energy anymore. In an extreme, cartoony, one-dimensional sense, that's what it could mean. But that's not realistic for most people working on their traumatized state.

There are probably going to be smaller steps toward unstuckness. It's probably not going to be that one-time home run of trauma releasing, the shaking and trembling kind of thing. It could happen, I suppose, but realistically, probably not. In my therapy practice, I find it's a longer process. It's not simply releasing your trauma all at once. There's a lot that goes into it, including building the safety state, which is a whole separate phase of this. Here, I'm focusing on the actual releasing of the stored or stuck trauma.

In my mind, unstuck really means less and less stuckness. The defensive state has less and less hold over you. There's less and less dysregulation over time. Hopefully quickly, sure, but it may be a longer process.

First you have to build the strength of your vagal brake. You have to build your distress tolerance. Then, once you have enough of that, and you can come from curiosity and interest and have the capacity to feel more of your stuck defensive state, you have to learn how to do that. And that's not exactly obvious.

So I don't think unstuck means you never experience it again. Maybe not as intensely. I hope not as intensely. That's definitely part of it. But I don't think it happens all at once. Here's what I'd expect instead:

ul: Less time spent in your defensive state.

More access to your safety state, and experiences like curiosity: being interested in what you have inside of you, interested in what it's like to be in a defensive state, not just emotionally but on a sensation level.
More capacity for self-reflection. That's part of the curiosity, looking inward.

More connection, with yourself, and potentially, or it should be, with other people. I don't think that means you become an extrovert who goes to parties all the time and hugs people nonstop. Connection could just be joining a local club, trying to meet new people, putting yourself out there in a different way.
More happiness, joy, and appreciation, hopefully, as you get more and more unstuck.

blocks.p: If you're trying to do some exercise or technique a guru taught you to get rid of your trauma or release it all at once, that doesn't tell me you're very curious about it. I'm sorry, but if that's where you're coming from, I want the best for you, and I don't hold a lot of hope that it's going to be super helpful.

If you're curious about what you have inside of you, then you can actually feel it, and then the body will naturally go through its self-regulation process. It releases the trauma, climbs the polyvagal ladder more and more, and builds more distress tolerance along the way. So curiosity, "Hey, what's going on inside of me? What is this truly like?", is part of the unstucking process. The next step would be to actually feel what it's like to have that stuck defensive state: the emotions that come with it, the thoughts, the sensations, and also the impulses, which I'll get to.

My heavily traumatized clients don't typically have that one major moment where all of a sudden they're unstuck and good to go. They definitely have moments of unstuckness, in session and out of session. But it feels like they take steps forward and then maybe some steps back, and forward again and then back. That's just part of change in general, and it's totally normal.

So unstuck is a gradual process. Does that mean you'll never experience that defensive state again? No, of course not. You're human. You're a mammal. You're going to feel these things again. Will you feel the trauma you're going through now, with flashbacks and all? I think the likelihood of that is less, and when it does come up, it won't be as intense. That's usually how it goes.

What I want you to get from this is that there may not be that home run. There may not be that one moment where a miracle happens and you're unstuck and you shake and tremble and release it all at once. That may not happen, and that's okay. Whatever process you're going through to find the relief you deserve, know that baby steps are completely okay. It's actually normal and good. It's forward.

The second question was about pendulation and titration leading to more self-regulation tools. First, let's talk briefly about what they are. Peter Levine has great information on pendulation and titration. If you read up on his work, you'll get a really good understanding of them.

Pendulation is going back and forth: from defense to safety, from your stuck, traumatized state to some sort of safety anchoring. You could think of it as going from pain to some sense of goodness, from bad to good. I don't look at it that way, because none of this is good or bad. It simply is. But it may feel negative or positive, so you're going from something that feels more painful to something that feels more pleasurable. You go back and forth, potentially rhythmically, potentially purposefully, where you're consciously choosing to go from one to the other.

Titration is feeling and releasing a little bit of your defensive state at a time. Say it's your stuck freeze state: you release a little bit at a time, not all at once. All at once is probably going to be overwhelming. It could trigger overwhelm or rage or panic if you're not prepared for it. So with titration, we're dipping in a bit at a time and climbing the polyvagal ladder a bit at a time. Pendulation is a part of the titration process. That's the basic idea.

To answer the question: pendulation and titration don't lead to self-regulation tools. They are self-regulation. The ability to go from discomfort to comfort, that is self-regulation. The ability to release a bit at a time, with patience and with curiosity, that is self-regulation.

It's a perfectly normal part of grief. When someone is grieving, they go from deep pain, missing that person, to remembering the last time they hugged them, or smiled together, or heard their laugh. Going from deep pain to deep connection is a natural process of pendulation. When I work with people in grief, they do it naturally. And what it does is titrate the pain they're going through, a bit at a time. It helps them climb their polyvagal ladder a little at a time.
So pendulation and titration are self-regulation. If we didn't get in each other's way, and we didn't get in our own way, that's how I think self-regulation would look.

So do they lead to self-regulation tools? Kind of, I guess, because the process can look different. Things like fidgeting, movement, using your imagination, and more can all be used in pendulation or titration.

Once you can anchor in safety, you can use that safety anchor as part of your pendulation process, once you're ready to actually feel the more painful stuff. If you know what brings you to safety, that can be part of pendulation. It will look different from mine. It's the same concept, the same self-regulation skill, but it looks different.

So you want to be able to anchor in safety, then pendulate to defense, and also from defense back into your safety state. If you can do that, it opens up the possibility of titration: releasing a bit of the trauma at a time.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.p: The third question is about impulses, and acting on them.

blocks.h3: From emotion to sensation to impulse

blocks.p: Start with the emotion you're experiencing. Maybe sadness, maybe anger, maybe anxiety. If you can experience that, then drill down a layer further, into the sensations underneath the emotion.

If you're experiencing the emotion of sadness, the sensation of sadness could be heaviness. It could be numbness. It could be feeling alone. It could be being in a dark room, not literally, or maybe literally, but more as the image that pops into your mind.

The sensations of the emotion are the experience of your stuck defensive state, or your current defensive state. Mindfully experiencing those sensations will potentially allow you to notice an impulse that surfaces from them.

So if you can go from the emotion down a layer into sensation, and then experience those sensations mindfully, watch them, listen to them, notice them, you may notice an impulse surface: something your body wants to do. There are steps to doing that, and I can't get into all of them here. But you have to be grounded in safety for this process to unfold. You have to be able to experience it mindfully.

Here's where I'll build on that. If you can't experience it mindfully, there's still kind of an impulse. Let's stick with sadness. Say you know you're sad. You know the emotion. But if you can't mindfully experience it, there's still something like an impulse. You still want to be alone. You might turn the lights off.

But that may be more of a behavioral adaptation, a reflex. That's the important point here. Take an impulse to shout, like in the question. Or there may be an impulse, a reflex, to eat, or to use a substance, or to drink. These feel like impulses, but that's not what I'm talking about. These are behavioral adaptations. They're reflexive, mindless, not mindful. An impulse is not the same as a reflexive behavioral adaptation.
So, speaking in general and not about this student in particular, what could a shout be?

ul: An attempt to release something stuck inside of you. Can you do it mindfully? Isn't there some kind of shouting therapy, where you scream into the air and you're supposed to feel better? That's one possibility.
An attempt to dominate somebody else and get them to submit to you, so that you can feel dominant.
A desperate attempt to get someone to hear you.

blocks.p: On that third one, if that's true, I'm more curious about the experience of being alone and being afraid. I'm more curious about the sensations that underlie the emotion of desperation and aloneness and needing help, and then the impulses that come from those. If that's true, there's some fear there, right? And with fear comes immobility, so shutdown.

So rather than focusing only on the behavior, whether it's shouting or using the drug or eating or cutting, it could be many things, I'm wondering what's underneath the behavior. Of course the behavior is significant. But what emotion is underneath it, and what sensations are underneath that emotion? There's always more underneath. If there's a desperate attempt to get someone to hear you through shouting, to me that means fear, and that means immobilization. If you can get to the level of feeling that, then an impulse may emerge from it.

blocks.h3: When the problem keeps coming back

blocks.p: Back to the question: "I keep thinking that acting on my impulse of shouting, for example, whenever I get caught up in a freeze state, will help release this frozen energy, but I keep falling back into this state."

If you're acting on what feels like an impulse and the problem keeps coming back, to me that reflects a behavioral adaptation, not an impulse that stems from your polyvagal state. If you're doing the same thing over and over again, acting on an impulse to yell at somebody, or to yell, or to use something to feel better, and the problem keeps surfacing, that's a behavioral adaptation.

If you can identify the true impulse, and mindfully act on it and experience it, then you have an opportunity to actually feel, and to allow the self-regulation process to happen: polyvagal ladder climbing, the defensive state releasing and discharging.
